SleepyHead: The Sleep Aid That Might Leave Havenfall Residents Awake… While Still Asleep

Havenfall Chronicles
Share:

SleepyHead: The Sleep Aid That Might Leave Havenfall Residents Awake… While Still Asleep

HAVENFALL — Most sleep aids make a fairly simple promise: take the medicine, close your eyes, and wake up feeling rested.

SleepyHead, however, has developed a rather unusual reputation.

The prescription insomnia medication has been used in Havenfall since the early years of the city, becoming a familiar name among residents struggling to fall asleep. But alongside its reputation as a powerful sleep aid, SleepyHead has become associated with some of the strangest nighttime incidents reported by patients.

People have described preparing and eating entire meals, making phone calls, shopping online, wandering outside, engaging in sexual activity, and even getting behind the wheel of a car — all while appearing to be asleep or only partially awake.

And perhaps the most unsettling part?

Many remember absolutely nothing the next morning.


When sleeping doesn't mean staying in bed


Doctors refer to these incidents as complex sleep behaviors — activities performed while a person is not fully awake.

Similar behaviors have been documented with several prescription insomnia medicines, particularly drugs in the sedative-hypnotic category. U.S. regulators have warned that some patients taking these medications have sleepwalked, prepared food, driven vehicles and performed other complicated activities without being fully conscious.

In some cases, the person can apparently hold conversations or operate objects normally enough that someone nearby may not immediately realize anything is wrong.

The person themselves may only discover what happened after waking up.

A half-eaten meal on the kitchen counter.
An online purchase they don't remember making.
A front door they don't remember opening.
Or, in the most frightening cases, a car that has somehow been moved.


The morning-after mystery


One of the most disturbing characteristics of these episodes is the memory loss.

According to medication safety information, people experiencing complex sleep behaviors commonly have little or no recollection of what happened afterward. Episodes can occur after the first dose or after someone has been taking the medication for some time.

That has created an unusual problem for Havenfall families.

How do you argue with someone about something they genuinely don't remember doing?

Some residents have reportedly woken up convinced they spent the entire night in bed, only to discover evidence suggesting otherwise.


And then there's the driving


Among the behaviors associated with certain insomnia medications, sleep-driving remains one of the most dangerous.

A person can apparently get out of bed, obtain their keys and operate a vehicle while not fully awake. Regulators have documented cases involving serious injuries and, in rare instances, deaths connected to complex sleep behaviors.

There is also a separate concern: next-morning impairment.

Even when someone is completely awake, medication remaining in the body can affect alertness, coordination and driving ability the following morning.

So for Havenfall residents taking SleepyHead, the question isn't always simply "Did I sleep?"

Sometimes it's:

"What did I do while I was sleeping?"


Havenfall's strangest sleep stories


The stories surrounding SleepyHead have become something of an urban legend in the city. Some are funny. Others are deeply unsettling.

One resident reportedly discovered that they had ordered hundreds of dollars worth of household products during the night.

Another supposedly woke up after finding food scattered across their kitchen despite having no memory of preparing anything.

And then there are the stories people don't laugh about — residents wandering outside, attempting to drive, or carrying out complicated activities they insist they would never consciously choose to do.

Medical authorities emphasize that these reactions are considered rare, but they can be serious.


The warning behind the strange stories


SleepyHead may have earned a bizarre reputation in Havenfall, but doctors warn residents not to treat these episodes as harmless entertainment.

People taking prescription sleep medication should follow their prescribed instructions, avoid combining medications or alcohol unless their healthcare professional says it is safe, and seek medical advice if they experience unusual nighttime behavior. Regulators specifically advise patients to stop certain insomnia medicines and contact their healthcare professional if they experience a complex sleep behavior.

Because sometimes the strangest part of sleep isn't what you dream about.

It's what you do after you fall asleep.

— Havenfall Chronicle
